On Oct. 27, Israelis will vote in their first national election since the Hamas attacks of Oct. 7, 2023. The vote is widely seen as a referendum on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Whether he or his more centrist competitor Gadi Eisenkot manage to pull ahead will determine not only the future of Israeli democracy but also its approach to Gaza and the West Bank, its relationship with the United States, and its standing abroad.
Dahlia Scheindlin is one of Israel’s leading political analysts and pollsters. As coalition bargaining unfolds, she will join FP Live to break down the political scenarios, what they mean for Israeli democracy, and how they could reshape Israel’s foreign policy.

Host and Guests

Dahlia Scheindlin

Political analyst

Dahlia Scheindlin is a public opinion expert and an international political and strategic consultant who has advised nine national campaigns in Israel and others in 15 other countries. She is the author of The Crooked Timber of Democracy in Israel, a columnist for Haaretz, and a founding member of +972 Magazine. Scheindlin is a former fellow at Century International, and she conducts the ongoing joint Israeli-Palestinian public opinion survey together with the Palestinian Center for Policy and Survey Research.

Where Ukraine Goes From Here

October 21, 2026

U.S. President Donald Trump’s so-called energy cease-fire hasn’t stopped Russia from bombing Ukrainian electricity and oil infrastructure. Nor has it stopped Ukraine from attacking Russian refineries. With winter approaching, Kyiv is racing to shore up its defenses and continue targeting Russia’s wartime economy—even as the United States begins to purchase Russian diesel. How should Kyiv’s strategy evolve? And how do the growing connections between Russia, Iran, China, and North Korea complicate matters? Andrea Kendall-Taylor is a former CIA analyst and expert on Russia and Eurasia at the Center for a New American Security. She joined FP’s Ravi Agrawal for a look at Ukraine’s diplomatic and battlefield options.

Why Spain Is Standing Up to Trump

October 14, 2026

Many countries have incorporated flattering U.S. President Donald Trump into their strategies for managing relations with the White House. Not Spain. Under Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, Madrid has clashed with the Trump administration on Iran, Israel, Venezuela, and funding NATO. Trump, for his part, has called Spain a “terrible partner” and threatened to cut off trade. Is Spain’s strategy working? Voters may decide for themselves, with a snap election called for Nov. 29. 
José Manuel Albares, Spain’s foreign minister and a longtime advisor to Sánchez, joined FP Live to discuss his country’s foreign policy.

The Scramble for AI Dominance

October 7, 2026

A spate of companies have recently held back their artificial intelligence models over safety concerns. First, Anthropic withheld Mythos. Then, OpenAI scrapped GPT-6.1 Astra’s launch. The very next day, U.S. President Donald Trump gathered AI executives to sign a voluntary accord to police themselves. The message? Any stricter regulation risks China catching the U.S. lead. But Matt Sheehan, co-director of the Carnegie Endowment’s China AI Initiative, points out that Beijing actually takes the opposite approach. It extensively regulates AI, and its companies are largely catching up with their American rivals anyway. Sheehan joined FP Live to discuss why the two AI superpowers govern the technology so differently and what the competition means for the future of geopolitics.

Can Development Work in Wartime?

October 2, 2026

How can you tackle poverty and create infrastructure amid an active conflict? Alexander De Croo is the head of the U.N. Development Program, and he joins FP’s Ravi Agrawal to make the case for spending development dollars on building long-term resilience. He’s exploring solutions to opium poppies in Afghanistan, electric grids in Ukraine, and sanitation in Gaza, even as major donors such as the United States pull back.
